column1: Patients and their caregivers are not uniform demand. Each carries realities - health, cognition, caregiver availability, life rhythm, and past experience with the agency - that shape what a good schedule looks like to them. Many of these are fixed and the schedule must bend to them, not the reverse. Realistic expectations differ by archetype: the same visit that reassures one patient frustrates another. Reading these drivers is how coordination stops failing the same patients repeatedly.

column1:
-  The sometime-Tuesday pattern: vague windows make patients wait all day, so they harden into narrow refusals to protect their time.
-  Missed-visit erosion: misses that are not acknowledged or quickly recovered turn into distrust, refusals, and limits on access.
-  New-face churn: continuity is not protected, so complex patients decline and generate more visits - a capacity drain the branch created.
-  Wrong-channel silence: reminders sent on a channel the patient cannot use read as no contact at all, breeding the anxiety reminders were meant to prevent.
column7:
-  Tight window plus on-my-way: patients get their day back, satisfaction rises, and failed visits fall.
-  Fast honest recovery: misses are owned and rebooked quickly, so trust survives the occasional failure.
-  Continuity protected: the same clinician means better outcomes, fewer crisis visits, and lower coordination load.
-  Right-channel reliability: contact reaches the patient the way that works, so confirmations actually land.

column1: Change-management read: a patient's expectations are set by their worst past experience with home health, not by your intentions. Make expectations explicit - a real window, the right channel, a known clinician - and bend the schedule to the fixed realities (caregiver availability, clinical timing, continuity) rather than treating them as negotiable. Reliability, repeated, is what converts a skeptical patient into a stable one.
